items.stem: Which unit is equivalent to the weber?
items.answer: T m²
items.markingKey: T m² (A1). Φ = BA.

items.stem: A student claims: "The flux through a coil is greatest when its plane is parallel to the field." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B).
items.markingKey: Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A flat coil is moved without rotating within a uniform field. Its flux linkage
items.answer: does not change
items.markingKey: B. B, A and θ are all unchanged.

items.stem: A loop of area 0.02 m² is in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The normal to the loop makes 60° with the field. What is the flux through the loop?
items.markingKey: B. Φ = BA cos θ = 0.00500 Wb; using sin θ gives the value for the angle measured from the plane.

items.stem: A coil of 200 turns, each of area 4.0 cm², lies perpendicular to a 0.1 T field. What is its flux linkage?
items.markingKey: B. NΦ = NBA = 0.00800 Wb.

items.stem: A search coil of 500 turns and area 1.2 cm² is connected to a charge-measuring meter; the total circuit resistance is 40 Ω. It is placed between the poles of a magnet with its plane perpendicular to the field and then pulled out quickly. A charge of 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ C flows. (a) Show that Q = Δ(NΦ)/R. (b) Determine the flux density between the poles. (c) Explain why the result does not depend on how quickly the coil is removed.
items.answer: (a) I = ε/R = Δ(NΦ)/(RΔt), Q = IΔt = Δ(NΦ)/R; (b) NBA = QR → B = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 40/(500 × 1.2 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.012 T; (c) faster removal gives larger current for a shorter time; the product (charge) depends only on the change in flux linkage.
items.markingKey: (a) I = ε/R = Δ(NΦ)/(RΔt), Q = IΔt = Δ(NΦ)/R; (b) NBA = QR → B = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 40/(500 × 1.2 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.012 T; (c) faster removal gives larger current for a shorter time; the product (charge) depends only on the change in flux linkage.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "magnetic flux"?
options: The emf ε = BvL induced across a straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B
The product of the magnetic flux density and the area perpendicular to it, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers (Wb)
The value of the steady (d.c.) voltage or current that would dissipate the same average power in a resistor, V_rms = V₀/√2 for a sine wave
The production of an emf in a conductor when the magnetic flux linking it changes
items.answer: The product of the magnetic flux density and the area perpendicular to it, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers (Wb)
items.markingKey: B. "magnetic flux" is the product of the magnetic flux density and the area perpendicular to it, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers (Wb).

items.stem: The flux through a loop is maximum when
options: the loop is at 45° to the field
the plane is parallel to the field
the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field
items.answer: the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field
items.markingKey: D. Normal parallel to B gives cos 0° = 1.

items.stem: Explain why flux linkage, rather than flux, determines the emf induced in a coil.
items.answer: Each turn has an emf −ΔΦ/Δt induced in it; the turns are in series so the emfs add, giving ε = −NΔΦ/Δt = −Δ(NΦ)/Δt.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each turn has an emf −ΔΦ/Δt induced in it; the turns are in series so the emfs add, giving ε = −NΔΦ/Δt = −Δ(NΦ)/Δt. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between flux linkage and flux.
items.answer: Flux is through one loop (BA cos θ); flux linkage is flux multiplied by the number of turns (NΦ).
items.markingKey: Flux is through one loop (BA cos θ); flux linkage is flux multiplied by the number of turns (NΦ). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes four statements while revising magnetic flux and flux linkage. Which one is a misconception?
options: 230 V is the rms value; the peak voltage is 230√2 ≈ 325 V.
The flux through a coil is greatest when its plane is parallel to the field.
Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.
More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged.
items.answer: The flux through a coil is greatest when its plane is parallel to the field.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B).

items.stem: A coil’s flux linkage is doubled by
options: rotating it to be parallel to the field
items.answer: doubling the number of turns
items.markingKey: A. NΦ ∝ N.

items.stem: A rectangular loop measuring 10 cm by 5.0 cm is placed in a uniform field of 0.40 T, with the normal to the loop at 30° to the field. Calculate the magnetic flux through the loop.
A loop of area 0.05 m² is in a uniform field of 0.4 T. The normal to the loop makes 30° with the field. What is the flux through the loop?
items.markingKey: C. Φ = BA cos θ = 0.0173 Wb; using sin θ gives the value for the angle measured from the plane.

items.stem: A 50-turn coil of area 4.0 cm² perpendicular to a 0.05 T field is turned so that its plane is parallel to the field. What is the change in flux linkage?
items.markingKey: D. NBA → 0: change = 0.00100 Wb.

items.stem: A circular coil of 250 turns and radius 1.5 cm is placed with its plane perpendicular to a field of 0.80 T. Calculate the flux linkage.

A square coil of side 5.0 cm and 100 turns is pulled at constant speed 0.20 m s⁻¹ through a region of uniform field 0.30 T that is 15 cm wide, with its plane perpendicular to the field. (a) Sketch the flux linkage against time from just before the coil enters until just after it leaves. (b) Calculate the maximum flux linkage. (c) Sketch and explain the corresponding emf–time graph.
items.answer: (a) flux linkage rises linearly for 0.25 s (entering), constant 0.075 Wb for 0.50 s (fully inside), falls linearly for 0.25 s; (b) NBA = 100 × 0.30 × 2.5 × 10⁻³ = 0.075 Wb; (c) emf = gradient = 0.30 V while entering, zero while fully inside, −0.30 V (opposite sign) while leaving.
items.markingKey: Correct shape with timings (A1 A1); NBA = 0.075 Wb (A1); emf = −d(NΦ)/dt = 0.30 V (M1); zero inside and reversed on exit (R1).

items.stem: "Faraday’s concept of field lines (flux) was essential to the development of electromagnetism." Discuss.
items.answer: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flux gave an intuitive picture leading to the law of induction; Maxwell built his equations on Faraday’s field ideas. Arguments against: the mathematics could in principle be developed without the picture; action-at-a-distance theories also predicted forces. Supported judgement: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS). Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "eddy currents".
items.answer: Induced currents that circulate within a conductor when the flux through it changes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: induced currents that circulate within a conductor when the flux through it changes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "An emf is only induced if the circuit is complete." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: An emf is induced whenever flux linkage changes; a complete circuit is needed only for a current to flow.
items.markingKey: An emf is induced whenever flux linkage changes; a complete circuit is needed only for a current to flow. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An induction hob heats a steel pan but not a glass pan because
options: the changing magnetic field induces eddy currents only in the conducting pan
steel has a higher melting point
items.answer: the changing magnetic field induces eddy currents only in the conducting pan
items.markingKey: A. Eddy currents need a conductor.

items.markingKey: B. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 15.0 V; forgetting N gives 0.0300 V.

items.stem: A 600-turn coil of area 6.0 cm² lies perpendicular to a 0.40 T field. The coil is flipped through 180° in 0.050 s. Calculate the average induced emf.
items.markingKey: Flux linkage changes from +NBA to −NBA: Δ(NΦ) = 2NBA (M1 A1); ε = 2NBA/Δt = 5.76 V (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Eddy currents are always undesirable."
items.answer: Undesirable in cores, but deliberately exploited in braking, heating and detection, so "always" is incorrect.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they cause energy loss in transformer cores and motors. Arguments against: they are used in induction braking for trains and rollercoasters; induction hobs and metal detectors rely on them; electromagnetic damping of meters. Supported judgement: Undesirable in cores, but deliberately exploited in braking, heating and detection, so "always" is incorrect.

items.stem: A small magnet is dropped from rest 60 cm above a short coil of 200 turns. As it passes through, the flux through each turn changes by about 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ Wb over a distance of 3.0 cm. (a) Estimate the speed of the magnet at the coil. (b) Estimate the average induced emf as it enters. (c) Explain why the emf pulse on leaving is larger and reversed. (d) Explain, using energy, why the magnet arrives slightly slower if the coil is connected to a resistor.
items.answer: (a) 3.43 m s⁻¹; (b) 6.86 V; (c) faster on leaving and flux decreasing instead of increasing; (d) energy transferred to the circuit comes from the magnet’s kinetic energy (Lenz’s law)
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) = 3.43 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) Δt ≈ L/v = 0.00874 s (M1); ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 6.86 V (A1). (c) greater speed → shorter time; ΔΦ reversed (R1 R1). (d) induced current opposes motion; work done against it becomes thermal energy in R (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produces it"?
items.answer: Lenz's law

items.stem: Use Lenz’s law to explain the direction of the induced current or force when the current in a nearby coil is switched on.
items.answer: The induced current flows in the opposite sense to the primary current, opposing the growth of flux.
items.markingKey: Changing flux identified (M1); induced effect opposes the change (R1); the induced current flows in the opposite sense to the primary current, opposing the growth of flux (A1).

items.stem: Distinguish between Lenz's law and Faraday's law.
items.answer: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the induced emf (rate of change of flux linkage); Lenz’s law gives its direction (opposing the change).
items.markingKey: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the induced emf (rate of change of flux linkage); Lenz’s law gives its direction (opposing the change). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila and a classmate in Lisbon disagree about Faraday's and Lenz's laws of electromagnetic induction. Which statement is correct?
options: Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.
The induced current always flows in the direction that helps the magnet move.
A generator coil produces maximum emf when it is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
A strong magnet held still next to a coil induces a large current.
items.answer: Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.

items.stem: Explain why the induced emf is larger when a coil with more turns is used.
items.answer: Each turn has the same rate of change of flux and so the same emf; the turns are in series, so the total emf is N times larger.

items.stem: Explain why a generator becomes harder to turn when more current is drawn from it.
items.answer: The current in the coil experiences a force in the magnetic field (motor effect) which, by Lenz’s law, opposes the rotation; larger current means larger opposing torque, so more mechanical work is needed – conservation of energy.

items.stem: A coil of 50 turns, area 0.02 m², rotates at 25 Hz in a field of 0.2 T. What is the peak emf?
items.markingKey: A. ε₀ = BANω = BAN(2πf) = 31.4 V.

items.stem: A generator coil of 200 turns, each of area 4.0 cm², rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.10 T. Calculate the peak and rms emf.
items.answer: ε₀ = 2.51 V; ε_rms = 1.78 V
items.markingKey: ω = 2πf = 314 rad s⁻¹ (A1); ε₀ = BANω = 2.51 V (M1 A1); ε_rms = ε₀/√2 = 1.78 V (A1).

items.stem: A coil of 100 turns, area 0.02 m², rotates at 25 Hz in a field of 0.2 T. What is the peak emf?
items.markingKey: B. ε₀ = BANω = BAN(2πf) = 62.8 V.

items.stem: "Generators violate conservation of energy because they produce electricity from magnets." Discuss.
items.answer: No violation: electrical energy comes from the mechanical work done against the opposing magnetic force.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the magnet itself is not used up. Arguments against: the energy comes from the mechanical work done to turn the coil; Lenz’s law opposition means work is needed whenever current flows; efficiency is always below 100 %. Supported judgement: No violation: electrical energy comes from the mechanical work done against the opposing magnetic force. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A conducting rod of length 0.25 m and mass 40 g slides without friction on horizontal rails connected by a 2.0 Ω resistor, in a vertical field of 0.80 T. It is pushed at a constant 3.0 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the induced emf and current. (b) Determine the force needed to keep it moving at constant speed. (c) Show that the mechanical power input equals the electrical power dissipated. (d) Describe the motion if the push is removed.
items.answer: (a) ε = BvL = 0.60 V; I = 0.30 A; (b) F = BIL = 0.060 N; (c) Fv = 0.18 W and I²R = 0.18 W; (d) the opposing force decelerates the rod; as v falls the force falls, so it slows with decreasing deceleration (exponentially) towards rest.
items.markingKey: ε = BvL (A1); I = ε/R (A1); F = BIL (M1 A1); power balance shown (R1); qualitative motion with reasoning (R1).

items.stem: Lenz’s law is a consequence of conservation of
items.answer: energy
items.markingKey: C. If the induced current aided the change, energy would be created.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "flux linkage".
items.answer: The product of the number of turns of a coil and the flux through each turn, NΦ, measured in Wb (or Wb-turns)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the product of the number of turns of a coil and the flux through each turn, NΦ, measured in Wb (or Wb-turns). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: The emf of an a.c. generator is maximum when the plane of the coil is
items.answer: parallel to the magnetic field
items.markingKey: C. Flux is then zero but changing fastest.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Lenz's law and Faraday's law.
items.answer: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the induced emf (rate of change of flux linkage); Lenz’s law gives its direction (opposing the change).
items.markingKey: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the induced emf (rate of change of flux linkage); Lenz’s law gives its direction (opposing the change). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Adding more turns increases the flux through a coil." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged.
items.markingKey: More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the emf of a rotating coil is zero when the flux through it is a maximum.
items.answer: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux; at the position of maximum flux (plane perpendicular to B) the flux–time graph is at a turning point, so its gradient – and the emf – is zero.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux; at the position of maximum flux (plane perpendicular to B) the flux–time graph is at a turning point, so its gradient – and the emf – is zero. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya is revising Faraday's and Lenz's laws of electromagnetic induction. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: An emf is only induced if the circuit is complete.
By Lenz’s law it opposes the change; helping it would create energy from nothing.
The induced current always flows in the direction that helps the magnet move.
The mains supply of 230 V means the voltage never exceeds 230 V.
items.answer: By Lenz’s law it opposes the change; helping it would create energy from nothing.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. By Lenz’s law it opposes the change; helping it would create energy from nothing.

items.stem: Explain why the angle in Φ = BA cos θ is measured between the field and the normal to the area.
items.answer: Only the component of B perpendicular to the surface passes through it; this is B cos θ when θ is the angle between B and the normal.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Only the component of B perpendicular to the surface passes through it; this is B cos θ when θ is the angle between B and the normal. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A slip-ring generator is changed to use a split-ring commutator. The output becomes
options: an a.c. emf of double frequency
items.answer: a rectified (one-direction) varying emf
items.markingKey: D. The commutator reverses connections every half-turn.

items.stem: The flux through each turn of a 500-turn coil changes by 0.00400 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the average induced emf?
items.markingKey: D. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 20.0 V; forgetting N gives 0.0400 V.

items.stem: A loop of area 0.01 m² is in a uniform field of 0.2 T. The normal to the loop makes 60° with the field. What is the flux through the loop?
items.markingKey: C. Φ = BA cos θ = 0.00100 Wb; using sin θ gives the value for the angle measured from the plane.

items.stem: A generator with a peak emf of 2.51 V (negligible internal resistance) is connected to a 100 Ω resistor. Calculate the rms current and the mean power dissipated.
Freya writes: "The induced current always flows in the direction that helps the magnet move." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: By Lenz’s law it opposes the change; helping it would create energy from nothing.
items.markingKey: By Lenz’s law it opposes the change; helping it would create energy from nothing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The flux through a coil is greatest when its plane is parallel to the field." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B).
items.markingKey: Flux is zero then; it is greatest when the plane is perpendicular to the field (normal parallel to B). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A generator coil produces maximum emf when it is perpendicular to the magnetic field." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest.
items.markingKey: Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The field through a 400-turn coil of area 2.0 cm² increases uniformly from 0 T to 0.50 T in 100 ms. The field is perpendicular to the coil. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Faraday’s concept of field lines (flux) was essential to the development of electromagnetism."
items.answer: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flux gave an intuitive picture leading to the law of induction; Maxwell built his equations on Faraday’s field ideas. Arguments against: the mathematics could in principle be developed without the picture; action-at-a-distance theories also predicted forces. Supported judgement: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Generators violate conservation of energy because they produce electricity from magnets."
items.answer: No violation: electrical energy comes from the mechanical work done against the opposing magnetic force.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the magnet itself is not used up. Arguments against: the energy comes from the mechanical work done to turn the coil; Lenz’s law opposition means work is needed whenever current flows; efficiency is always below 100 %. Supported judgement: No violation: electrical energy comes from the mechanical work done against the opposing magnetic force. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A small magnet is dropped from rest 40 cm above a short coil of 1000 turns. As it passes through, the flux through each turn changes by about 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ Wb over a distance of 2.0 cm. (a) Estimate the speed of the magnet at the coil. (b) Estimate the average induced emf as it enters. (c) Explain why the emf pulse on leaving is larger and reversed. (d) Explain, using energy, why the magnet arrives slightly slower if the coil is connected to a resistor.
items.answer: (a) 2.80 m s⁻¹; (b) 28.0 V; (c) faster on leaving and flux decreasing instead of increasing; (d) energy transferred to the circuit comes from the magnet’s kinetic energy (Lenz’s law)
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(2gh) = 2.80 m s⁻¹ (A1). (b) Δt ≈ L/v = 0.00714 s (M1); ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 28.0 V (A1). (c) greater speed → shorter time; ΔΦ reversed (R1 R1). (d) induced current opposes motion; work done against it becomes thermal energy in R (R1).

items.stem: "Flux linkage is just a mathematical convenience with no physical meaning." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is a physically meaningful quantity because its rate of change is what is measured as induced emf.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: NΦ can be computed without picturing field lines. Arguments against: it directly determines the induced emf through Faraday’s law; search coils measure changes in flux linkage; it links to measurable charge flow Q = Δ(NΦ)/R. Supported judgement: It is a physically meaningful quantity because its rate of change is what is measured as induced emf. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "electromagnetic induction"?
options: The product of the number of turns of a coil and the flux through each turn, NΦ, measured in Wb (or Wb-turns)
The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produces it
The maximum value of a sinusoidal emf, ε₀ = BANω for a rotating coil
The production of an emf in a conductor when the magnetic flux linking it changes
items.answer: The production of an emf in a conductor when the magnetic flux linking it changes
items.markingKey: D. "electromagnetic induction" is the production of an emf in a conductor when the magnetic flux linking it changes.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The unit of magnetic flux; 1 Wb = 1 T m²"?
items.answer: weber
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of weber.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "motional emf"?
options: A device in which a coil rotates in a magnetic field, producing a sinusoidal emf ε = BANω sin ωt
The direction of an induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produces it
The emf ε = BvL induced across a straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B
The maximum value of a sinusoidal emf, ε₀ = BANω for a rotating coil
items.answer: The emf ε = BvL induced across a straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B
items.markingKey: C. "motional emf" is the emf ε = BvL induced across a straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B.

items.stem: Explain, using Lenz’s law, why work must be done to push a magnet into a coil connected in a closed circuit.
items.answer: The induced current makes the coil end facing the magnet a like pole, which repels the approaching magnet; work must be done against this force, and that work becomes the electrical energy dissipated in the circuit.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The induced current makes the coil end facing the magnet a like pole, which repels the approaching magnet; work must be done against this force, and that work becomes the electrical energy dissipated in the circuit. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Jonas is revising magnetic flux and flux linkage. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The induced current always flows in the direction that helps the magnet move.
More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged.
The flux through a coil is greatest when its plane is parallel to the field.
Adding more turns increases the flux through a coil.
items.answer: More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. More turns increase the flux linkage NΦ; the flux through each turn is unchanged.

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship ε = BvL for a rod moving at different speeds on rails is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot ε (y-axis) against v (x-axis); gradient = BL, from which B can be found. A non-zero intercept would suggest a contact emf or meter offset.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: ε against v (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = BL, from which B can be found (A1). A non-zero intercept would suggest a contact emf or meter offset.

items.stem: Use Lenz’s law to explain the direction of the induced current or force when a metal plate swings as a pendulum between the poles of a magnet.
items.answer: Eddy currents in the plate produce forces opposing its motion, so the swing is damped quickly.
items.markingKey: Changing flux identified (M1); induced effect opposes the change (R1); eddy currents in the plate produce forces opposing its motion, so the swing is damped quickly (A1).

items.stem: Explain the difference between magnetic flux density and magnetic flux.
items.answer: Flux density B (T) is the field strength at a point; flux Φ = BA cos θ (Wb) is the total "amount" of field passing through a given area.
items.markingKey: Flux density B (T) is the field strength at a point; flux Φ = BA cos θ (Wb) is the total "amount" of field passing through a given area. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tomás is revising induced emf in moving conductors and rotating coils; AC generators. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The induced current always flows in the direction that helps the magnet move.
A strong magnet held still next to a coil induces a large current.
Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest.
Adding more turns increases the flux through a coil.
items.answer: Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest.
items.markingKey: C. The other options are common misconceptions. Maximum emf occurs when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where flux changes fastest.

items.stem: Lars writes: "A strong magnet held still next to a coil induces a large current." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong.
items.markingKey: Induction requires a changing flux; a stationary magnet induces nothing, however strong. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A coil of 100 turns, each of area 4.0 cm², lies perpendicular to a 0.05 T field. What is its flux linkage?
items.markingKey: A. NΦ = NBA = 0.00200 Wb.

items.stem: A coil of 50 turns, area 0.02 m², rotates at 50 Hz in a field of 0.2 T. What is the peak emf?
items.markingKey: A. ε₀ = BANω = BAN(2πf) = 62.8 V.

items.stem: The flux through each turn of a 200-turn coil changes by 0.00600 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the average induced emf?
items.markingKey: C. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 12.0 V; forgetting N gives 0.0600 V.

items.stem: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries 0.50 A. A small coil of 30 turns and area 5.0 cm² is placed inside, coaxial with the solenoid. Determine the flux linkage of the small coil.
A generator with a peak emf of 1.26 V (negligible internal resistance) is connected to a 100 Ω resistor. Calculate the rms current and the mean power dissipated.
The flux through each turn of a 500-turn coil changes by 0.00400 Wb in 0.2 s. What is the average induced emf?
items.markingKey: B. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 10.0 V; forgetting N gives 0.0200 V.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Faraday’s concept of field lines (flux) was essential to the development of electromagnetism."
items.answer: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flux gave an intuitive picture leading to the law of induction; Maxwell built his equations on Faraday’s field ideas. Arguments against: the mathematics could in principle be developed without the picture; action-at-a-distance theories also predicted forces. Supported judgement: Faraday’s visual model was a crucial creative step that guided Maxwell, an example of models driving theory (NOS).

items.stem: "Alternating current is better than direct current for transmitting electrical energy over long distances." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: A.c. dominates grids because of transformers, but HVDC is better for very long or undersea links; the choice depends on distance and cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: transformers make it easy to step a.c. up to high voltage, reducing I²R losses. Arguments against: HVDC links now carry power over very long distances and undersea with lower losses; a.c. has reactive losses and skin effect; d.c. avoids synchronisation problems. Supported judgement: A.c. dominates grids because of transformers, but HVDC is better for very long or undersea links; the choice depends on distance and cost. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem:
A search coil of 200 turns is placed in a field that increases at a controlled rate dB/dt; the induced emf ε is measured. Theory: ε = NA dB/dt.

dB/dt / T s⁻¹ | ε / mV
0.05 | 4.86
0.10 | 9.84
0.15 | 14.79
0.20 | 19.54
0.25 | 25.45
0.30 | 30.39

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the cross-sectional area of the coil. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the area with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) ε in V (y) against dB/dt (x); (b) gradient ≈ 0.102 V s T⁻¹; (c) 5.12 × 10⁻⁴ m²; (d) 5.12 × 10⁻⁴ m² ± 2 × 10⁻⁵ m²
items.markingKey: (a) ε in V (y) against dB/dt (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.102 V s T⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) A = gradient/N = 5.12 × 10⁻⁴ m² (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m²; value quoted to the same precision (A1).
